content_units: California Classification Snapshot
Based on the facts you gave, this looks like   high employee-classification risk   if the bakery is treating the cake decorator as an independent contractor in California.
California generally applies the   ABC test   for many wage-order and Labor Code purposes. On your facts, the decorator likely points toward   employee status  , not contractor status:
-   A — Freedom from control:   likely   fails
-   B — Work outside the usual course of business:   likely   fails
-   C — Independently established trade/business:   likely   weak or fails   based on the facts provided
California Misclassification Risk Checklist
Factor   Your Facts   Risk Signal   Why It Matters
Control over work   Fixed schedule   High   Set hours strongly suggest employer control
Tools/equipment   Uses bakery's tools   High   Employees often use company tools; contractors often use their own
Core business work   Cake decorating for a bakery   Very High   This appears inside the bakery's usual course of business
Right to delegate   Cannot send substitute   High   Contractors often control staffing or can subcontract
Pay structure   Hourly, every two weeks   High   Hourly payroll-style payment looks more like employment
Ongoing relationship   30 hours/week since 2025-02-01   High   Regular, continuing service resembles a part-time employee
Independent business signs   Not stated   Medium-High   Missing signs of a separate business weakens contractor position
Likely Bottom Line

The biggest issue is   Part B of the ABC test  : a bakery hiring a cake decorator is hiring someone to perform the bakery's   main line of business  , which is usually a strong indicator of   employee status  .
Red Flags the Bakery Should Treat Seriously
Option 1:   Core-business mismatch     Cake decorating is central to bakery operations, not a separate outside specialty     Strongest employee indicator
Option 2:   Schedule and supervision     Fixed weekly hours suggest the bakery controls when work is done     Control risk
Option 3:   Hourly pay cadence     Hourly pay every two weeks resembles wages rather than project-based billing     Payroll-style relationship
Option 4:   No substitute allowed     If only that person can perform the work, the worker looks integrated into staff     Personal-service dependence
Option 5:   Bakery tools and workspace     Using the bakery's equipment and likely working onsite suggests integration into the business     Operational integration
Practical Risk View
If the bakery has been calling this person a contractor, a lawyer or accountant will likely want to examine:
- Whether wages, overtime, meal/rest break compliance, and payroll taxes should have applied
- Whether a   W-2 employee setup   should have been used instead of   1099   treatment
- Whether any back-pay, penalty, workers' compensation, unemployment, or tax exposure exists
Records to Gather Before Talking to a Lawyer or Accountant
Collect and organize these in one folder, ideally by month:
-   Written agreement
- Independent contractor agreement, offer letter, emails, texts, or onboarding messages
-   Work schedule records
- Shift calendars, time logs, texts assigning hours, punch records, weekly rosters
-   Pay records
- Invoices, pay stubs, payroll records, checks, direct-deposit reports, 1099 forms, W-9, rate confirmations
-   Work instructions
- Training materials, decorating standards, supervisor messages, checklists, required procedures
-   Tool/equipment records
- Proof the bakery supplied tools, uniforms, ingredients, workspace, storage, or POS/login access
-   Business-integration records
- Menus, website pages, ads, custom cake offerings, job posts, org charts showing cake decorating as a bakery service
-   Exclusivity/availability evidence
- Any rule limiting outside work, noncompete-style language, or expectations of ongoing availability
-   Substitution/delegation evidence
- Messages or policy showing the decorator could not send another person
-   Tax and insurance records
- Payroll tax filings, 1099 filings, workers' comp policy info, unemployment account records
-   Hour-and-break records
- Daily start/end times, meal breaks, rest breaks, overtime patterns, weekend/holiday work
-   Licensing/business-status documents
- Any decorator business license, LLC filings, business cards, website, separate client list, insurance certificate, advertising
-   Communications about role
- Messages describing them as “staff,” “employee,” “team member,” or requiring manager approval for time off
What a Lawyer or Accountant Will Likely Focus On
-   ABC Test
-   A:   Was the decorator truly free from the bakery's control?
-   B:   Was cake decorating outside the bakery's usual business? On these facts, likely no.
-   C:   Did the decorator operate an established independent business serving multiple clients?
-   Money exposure areas
- Unpaid overtime
- Missed meal/rest break premiums
- Payroll taxes and withholding
- Workers' compensation and unemployment contributions
- Wage-statement and final-pay issues
- Potential penalties tied to misclassification
-   Status correction planning
- Whether to convert the role to employee status going forward
- Whether past payments need cleanup or amended reporting
- Whether contracts and onboarding documents need revision for future hires
Quick Actions
Review CA ABC Test
Organize Worker File
